title: SaaS Validation Before You Build
audience: Independent developers with a plausible SaaS idea who want evidence before committing weeks or months to building it.
shortDescription: Test the customer, problem, urgency, and willingness to act before technical momentum turns an assumption into a product roadmap.
coreOutcome: Make an evidence-based build, change, or stop decision before heavy development begins.
problem: You can build the software, which makes it dangerously easy to treat a plausible idea as validated demand.
hook: Being able to build the product quickly is not a reason to skip finding out whether anyone cares.
reframe: Technical founders have a specific validation problem: building feels productive, measurable, and familiar. Talking to potential customers feels slower and less certain. That makes it easy to spend a month proving that the software can exist while the riskiest assumptions remain untouched. Who has the problem? How often does it happen? What does it cost them now? Are they already trying to solve it? Will they invest time, access, attention, or money to change the situation? Encouraging comments do not answer those questions. SaaS Validation Before You Build turns the idea into falsifiable assumptions and then looks for behavioral evidence strong enough to justify the next investment. You define the audience and problem narrowly enough to test, run focused conversations and commitment tests, record what people actually do, and decide in advance what evidence means build, revise, or stop. The purpose is not to create certainty. It is to make the cost of being wrong much smaller than building the full product first.

delivery.length: Implementation guide for assumption mapping, customer research, problem evidence, commitment tests, and build decisions.
delivery.worksheets: Riskiest-assumption map, interview guide, evidence log, commitment-test design, decision thresholds, and build-change-stop review.
delivery.time: Run the validation process before committing to heavy product development or a large MVP scope.

proof.title: Compliments and commitments are recorded differently.
proof.body: The system separates statements such as “I would use that” from actions that cost the prospect something, such as giving access to a workflow, joining a pilot, introducing a decision-maker, or paying.
proof.before: Several people said the idea sounds useful, so start building the MVP.
proof.after: Define the risky assumption, choose the evidence that would support or weaken it, run the test, record behavior, and make the build decision against a threshold set in advance.

situation: The idea feels plausible, but customer, problem, urgency, alternatives, and willingness-to-act assumptions remain largely untested.
commonFailure: Feature planning, prototype enthusiasm, and friendly feedback can feel like progress without producing evidence that supports a commercial build decision.
methodology: State falsifiable assumptions, identify the riskiest ones, collect problem evidence, test commitment with appropriate asks, record behavior, and compare the results with explicit build, revise, or stop criteria.
capabilities: Identify the assumptions most likely to make the product fail commercially
Run focused customer conversations and commitment tests
Use evidence thresholds to decide whether to build, change, or stop
contents: Audience definition and reachable early-customer selection
Problem interviews that separate evidence from encouragement
Current alternatives, switching friction, urgency, and problem cost
Commitment tests using time, access, introductions, pilots, or payment where appropriate
Build, revise, or stop thresholds set before the result is known
Validation review and handoff into MVP scope
whoItsFor: Indie and bootstrapped SaaS builders before heavy development
Developers who have an idea but little behavioral evidence from potential customers
Technical founders who want a disciplined reason to build instead of relying on enthusiasm
whoItsNotFor: Anyone seeking certainty or guaranteed product-market fit
Products that already have strong customer evidence and have earned the build decision
Anyone unwilling to talk to real potential customers or test commitment

faqs.question: Do I need a prototype first?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Many risky assumptions concern the customer and problem, and those can often be tested before a working product exists.

faqs.question: How many interviews prove the idea?
faqs.answer: No fixed interview count proves demand. The guide focuses on evidence quality, repeated patterns, contradictory evidence, and commitment rather than a magic sample size.

faqs.question: Does validation guarantee the SaaS will work?
faqs.answer: No. It reduces avoidable uncertainty before a larger investment. Product, pricing, acquisition, retention, and execution still have to work afterward.

faqs.question: What happens if the evidence is weak?
faqs.answer: You revise the audience, problem, or proposed approach, run a better test, or stop. A cheap no is a useful result when the alternative is months of building.
